import Mathlib

/-!
# The Pickover–Clifford Attractor Family

The Clifford (a.k.a. Pickover–Clifford) attractor is the planar discrete dynamical
system generated by iterating the map

  `F(x, y) = (sin(a·y) + c·cos(a·x),  sin(b·x) + d·cos(b·y))`

with real parameters `a b c d`.  It is one of the classic "strange attractor"
families.  This file develops a rigorous, machine-checked theory of its basic
analytic structure:

1. **Boundedness of the image.** Every output coordinate is trapped in an explicit
   interval determined by the parameters: `|F(p).1| ≤ 1 + |c|` and
   `|F(p).2| ≤ 1 + |d|`.
2. **Trapping region / forward invariance.** The explicit box
   `[-(1+|c|), 1+|c|] × [-(1+|d|), 1+|d|]` absorbs the whole plane in one step and
   is therefore forward invariant.  Every orbit lands inside it after one step.
3. **Lipschitz estimate.** `F` is globally Lipschitz with constant
   `L = max (|a|(1+|c|)) (|b|(1+|d|))` for the sup metric on `ℝ × ℝ`.
4. **Contraction regime.** When `L < 1`, `F` is a contraction, hence has a unique
   fixed point, and *every* orbit converges to it.  In this parameter regime the
   "attractor" degenerates to a single globally attracting point.

## Main results

* `cliffordMap_fst_abs_le`, `cliffordMap_snd_abs_le` — coordinate boundedness.
* `cliffordMap_mapsTo_box` — the whole plane maps into the trapping box.
* `cliffordMap_forward_invariant` — the box is forward invariant.
* `cliffordMap_iterate_mem_box` — every orbit is in the box after one step.
* `cliffordMap_dist_le` — the global Lipschitz (sup-metric) estimate.
* `cliffordMap_exists_unique_fixedPoint` — unique fixed point in the contraction regime.
* `cliffordMap_tendsto_fixedPoint` — global convergence in the contraction regime.

## References

* C. A. Pickover, *Computers, Pattern, Chaos and Beauty* (1990).
* P. Clifford, attractor formulas popularised in the chaos-art literature.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis H1: the Clifford map, being a sum of a bounded trig term and a
--   parameter-scaled bounded trig term, has each coordinate bounded by 1 + |param|.
--   CONFIRMED: clean triangle-inequality argument (abs_add_le + abs_sin/cos_le_one).
-- Hypothesis H2: the explicit box is not merely invariant but *absorbing* — the
--   image of ALL of ℝ² already lies inside it.  CONFIRMED: H2 is strictly stronger
--   than forward invariance and is what makes the attractor compact.
-- Hypothesis H3: in the small-parameter regime the strange attractor is an
--   artefact; the dynamics collapse to a single point.  CONFIRMED via the sup-metric
--   Lipschitz constant L = max(|a|(1+|c|), |b|(1+|d|)) and Banach's fixed-point
--   theorem (ContractingWith).  Insight: the cross-coupling terms (c·cos(a·x),
--   d·cos(b·y)) are what inflate the Lipschitz constant beyond |a|,|b|, so large |c|
--   or |d| destroy contraction even for small |a|,|b|.
-- Failure analysis: an earlier attempt to bound the Lipschitz constant by
--   max(|a|,|b|) alone is FALSE — it ignores the parameter-scaled coupling and
--   would wrongly predict contraction for, e.g., a=b=0.4, c=d=5.
-/

open Real

noncomputable section

namespace Clifford

/-- The Pickover–Clifford attractor map on the plane (with sup metric via `Prod`). -/
def cliffordMap (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) : ℝ × ℝ :=
  (Real.sin (a * p.2) + c * Real.cos (a * p.1),
   Real.sin (b * p.1) + d * Real.cos (b * p.2))

/-- The explicit trapping box of the Clifford map. -/
def cliffordBox (c d : ℝ) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  {p | |p.1| ≤ 1 + |c| ∧ |p.2| ≤ 1 + |d|}

/-
The first coordinate of the Clifford map is bounded by `1 + |c|`.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_fst_abs_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    |(cliffordMap a b c d p).1| ≤ 1 + |c| := by
  unfold cliffordMap;
  exact abs_le.mpr ⟨ by cases abs_cases c <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_sin_le_one ( a * p.2 ) ), abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_cos_le_one ( a * p.1 ) ) ], by cases abs_cases c <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_sin_le_one ( a * p.2 ) ), abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_cos_le_one ( a * p.1 ) ) ] ⟩

/-
The second coordinate of the Clifford map is bounded by `1 + |d|`.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_snd_abs_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    |(cliffordMap a b c d p).2| ≤ 1 + |d| := by
  unfold cliffordMap;
  exact abs_le.mpr ⟨ by cases abs_cases d <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_sin_le_one ( b * p.1 ) ), abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_cos_le_one ( b * p.2 ) ) ], by cases abs_cases d <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_sin_le_one ( b * p.1 ) ), abs_le.mp ( Real.abs_cos_le_one ( b * p.2 ) ) ] ⟩

/-
The Clifford map sends the entire plane into the trapping box: the box is
*absorbing*.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_mapsTo_box (a b c d : ℝ) :
    Set.MapsTo (cliffordMap a b c d) Set.univ (cliffordBox c d) := by
  intro p _; exact ⟨ cliffordMap_fst_abs_le a b c d p, cliffordMap_snd_abs_le a b c d p ⟩ ;

/-
The trapping box is forward invariant under the Clifford map.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_forward_invariant (a b c d : ℝ) :
    Set.MapsTo (cliffordMap a b c d) (cliffordBox c d) (cliffordBox c d) := by
  exact Set.MapsTo.mono_left (cliffordMap_mapsTo_box a b c d) (Set.subset_univ _)

/-
Every orbit lands inside the trapping box after a single step.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_iterate_mem_box (a b c d : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (p : ℝ × ℝ) :
    (cliffordMap a b c d)^[n] p ∈ cliffordBox c d := by
  rcases n with ( _ | n ) <;> simp_all +decide [ Function.iterate_succ_apply' ];
  exact ⟨ cliffordMap_fst_abs_le a b c d _, cliffordMap_snd_abs_le a b c d _ ⟩

/-
Global Lipschitz (sup-metric) estimate for the Clifford map.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_dist_le (a b c d : ℝ) (p q : ℝ × ℝ) :
    dist (cliffordMap a b c d p) (cliffordMap a b c d q) ≤
      max (|a| * (1 + |c|)) (|b| * (1 + |d|)) * dist p q := by
  refine' max_le_iff.mpr ⟨ _, _ ⟩;
  · -- Apply the triangle inequality and the bounds on the sine and cosine functions.
    have h1 : abs ((Real.sin (a * p.2) + c * Real.cos (a * p.1)) - (Real.sin (a * q.2) + c * Real.cos (a * q.1))) ≤ abs a * abs (p.2 - q.2) + abs c * abs a * abs (p.1 - q.1) := by
      -- Apply the triangle inequality to the expression.
      have h_triangle : abs (Real.sin (a * p.2) - Real.sin (a * q.2)) ≤ abs a * abs (p.2 - q.2) ∧ abs (Real.cos (a * p.1) - Real.cos (a * q.1)) ≤ abs a * abs (p.1 - q.1) := by
        have h_lip : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.sin x - Real.sin y| ≤ |x - y| ∧ |Real.cos x - Real.cos y| ≤ |x - y| := by
          have h_lip : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.sin x - Real.sin y| ≤ |x - y| := by
            grind +suggestions
          have h_lip_cos : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.cos x - Real.cos y| ≤ |x - y| := by
            intro x y; have := h_lip ( x + π / 2 ) ( y + π / 2 ) ; simp_all +decide [ Real.sin_add ] ;
          exact fun x y => ⟨h_lip x y, h_lip_cos x y⟩;
        exact ⟨ le_trans ( h_lip _ _ |>.1 ) ( by rw [ ← abs_mul ] ; ring_nf; norm_num ), le_trans ( h_lip _ _ |>.2 ) ( by rw [ ← abs_mul ] ; ring_nf; norm_num ) ⟩;
      exact abs_le.mpr ⟨ by cases abs_cases c <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp h_triangle.1, abs_le.mp h_triangle.2 ], by cases abs_cases c <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp h_triangle.1, abs_le.mp h_triangle.2 ] ⟩;
    refine' le_trans h1 _;
    rw [ Prod.dist_eq ];
    rw [ Real.dist_eq, Real.dist_eq ];
    cases max_cases ( |a| * ( 1 + |c| ) ) ( |b| * ( 1 + |d| ) ) <;> cases max_cases |p.1 - q.1| |p.2 - q.2| <;> nlinarith [ abs_nonneg a, abs_nonneg c, abs_nonneg ( p.1 - q.1 ), abs_nonneg ( p.2 - q.2 ), mul_nonneg ( abs_nonneg a ) ( abs_nonneg c ), mul_nonneg ( abs_nonneg a ) ( abs_nonneg ( p.1 - q.1 ) ), mul_nonneg ( abs_nonneg a ) ( abs_nonneg ( p.2 - q.2 ) ) ];
  · -- Apply the triangle inequality to the second component.
    have h2 : abs (Real.sin (b * p.1) - Real.sin (b * q.1)) ≤ abs b * abs (p.1 - q.1) ∧ abs (Real.cos (b * p.2) - Real.cos (b * q.2)) ≤ abs b * abs (p.2 - q.2) := by
      -- Apply the mean value theorem to the sine and cosine functions.
      have h_sin : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.sin x - Real.sin y| ≤ |x - y| := by
        grind +suggestions
      have h_cos : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.cos x - Real.cos y| ≤ |x - y| := by
        intro x y; rw [ ← Real.sin_pi_div_two_sub, ← Real.sin_pi_div_two_sub ] ; simpa [ abs_sub_comm ] using h_sin ( Real.pi / 2 - x ) ( Real.pi / 2 - y ) ;
      exact ⟨ le_trans ( h_sin _ _ ) ( by rw [ ← abs_mul ] ; ring_nf; norm_num ), le_trans ( h_cos _ _ ) ( by rw [ ← abs_mul ] ; ring_nf; norm_num ) ⟩;
    -- Apply the triangle inequality to the second component and use the bounds from h2.
    have h2_bound : abs ((cliffordMap a b c d p).2 - (cliffordMap a b c d q).2) ≤ abs b * (abs (p.1 - q.1) + abs d * abs (p.2 - q.2)) := by
      simp_all +decide [ mul_add, cliffordMap ];
      exact abs_le.mpr ⟨ by cases abs_cases d <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp h2.1, abs_le.mp h2.2 ], by cases abs_cases d <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp h2.1, abs_le.mp h2.2 ] ⟩;
    refine' le_trans h2_bound _;
    refine' le_trans _ ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right ( le_max_right _ _ ) ( dist_nonneg ) );
    rw [ mul_assoc ];
    exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( by rw [ add_mul, one_mul ] ; exact add_le_add ( by exact le_max_left _ _ ) ( mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( by exact le_max_right _ _ ) ( abs_nonneg _ ) ) ) ( abs_nonneg _ )

/-
In the contraction regime `L < 1`, the Clifford map has a unique fixed point.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_exists_unique_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ)
    (h : max (|a| * (1 + |c|)) (|b| * (1 + |d|)) < 1) :
    ∃! p : ℝ × ℝ, cliffordMap a b c d p = p := by
  -- By the formula for metric distance on ℝ × ℝ, this is equivalent to L = max (|a| * (1 + |c|)) (|b| * (1 + |d|)).
  -- Hence, we can conclude that L < 1.
  have h1 : ∃ K : NNReal, K < 1 ∧ ∀ p q : ℝ × ℝ, dist (cliffordMap a b c d p) (cliffordMap a b c d q) ≤ K * dist p q := by
    refine' ⟨ ⟨ _, _ ⟩, _, _ ⟩;
    exacts [ Max.max ( |a| * ( 1 + |c| ) ) ( |b| * ( 1 + |d| ) ), by positivity, h, fun p q => by simpa using cliffordMap_dist_le a b c d p q ];
  choose K hK₁ hK₂ using h1;
  -- Let $q$ be the unique fixed point of $f$.
  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ : ∃ q : ℝ × ℝ, cliffordMap a b c d q = q := by
    -- By the properties of the contraction mapping, there exists a unique fixed point.
    have h_fixed_point : ∃ q : ℝ × ℝ, Function.IsFixedPt (cliffordMap a b c d) q := by
      have h_contractive : ContractingWith K (cliffordMap a b c d) := by
        exact ⟨ hK₁, LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul hK₂ ⟩
      exact ⟨ _, h_contractive.fixedPoint_isFixedPt ⟩;
    exact h_fixed_point;
  refine' ⟨ q, hq, fun p hp => _ ⟩;
  contrapose! hK₂;
  exact ⟨ p, q, by simpa [ hp, hq ] using mul_lt_of_lt_one_left ( dist_pos.mpr hK₂ ) ( show ( K : ℝ ) < 1 from hK₁ ) ⟩

/-
In the contraction regime, every orbit converges to the unique fixed point.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_tendsto_fixedPoint (a b c d : ℝ)
    (h : max (|a| * (1 + |c|)) (|b| * (1 + |d|)) < 1) (p₀ : ℝ × ℝ) :
    ∃ q : ℝ × ℝ, cliffordMap a b c d q = q ∧
      Filter.Tendsto (fun n => (cliffordMap a b c d)^[n] p₀) Filter.atTop (nhds q) := by
  -- Let L := max (|a|*(1+|c|)) (|b|*(1+|d|)) ≥ 0, K := L.toNNReal with (K:ℝ)=L. Build ContractingWith K (cliffordMap a b c d) := ⟨hK1, LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul (by simpa using cliffordMap_dist_le a b c d)⟩ where hK1 : K < 1 from h.
  set K : NNReal := ⟨max (|a| * (1 + |c|)) (|b| * (1 + |d|)), by
    positivity⟩
  generalize_proofs at *;
  have h_contracting : ContractingWith K (cliffordMap a b c d) := by
    constructor;
    · exact h;
    · rw [ lipschitzWith_iff_dist_le_mul ];
      convert cliffordMap_dist_le a b c d using 1;
  exact ⟨ _, h_contracting.fixedPoint_isFixedPt, h_contracting.tendsto_iterate_fixedPoint p₀ ⟩

/-!
-- !-- Lab Notes (cycle 2) -- !--
-- Hypothesis H4 (Conjecture 4 of FUTURE_DIRECTIONS): in the diagonally symmetric
--   regime a = b and c = d, any fixed point lies on the diagonal x = y.
-- Experiment: subtract the two fixed-point equations,
--   p.1 - p.2 = (sin(a·p.2) - sin(a·p.1)) + c·(cos(a·p.1) - cos(a·p.2)),
--   bound the RHS by the same Lipschitz constant L = |a|(1+|c|) < 1, giving
--   |p.1 - p.2| ≤ L·|p.1 - p.2|, hence (1 - L)|p.1 - p.2| ≤ 0, forcing p.1 = p.2.
-- CONFIRMED: the proof needs only L < 1 (contraction regime) and is independent of
--   the Banach machinery — a purely algebraic squeeze.  Insight: the diagonal is an
--   invariant line, and contraction pins the fixed point to it.
-/

/-
In the diagonally symmetric regime `a = b`, `c = d` with `L = |a|(1+|c|) < 1`,
every fixed point of the Clifford map lies on the diagonal `x = y`.
-/
theorem cliffordMap_symmetric_fixedPoint_on_diagonal (a c : ℝ)
    (h : |a| * (1 + |c|) < 1) (p : ℝ × ℝ) (hp : cliffordMap a a c c p = p) :
    p.1 = p.2 := by
  -- Apply the triangle inequality and the Lipschitz property of sine and cosine.
  have h_lip : |Real.sin (a * p.2) - Real.sin (a * p.1)| ≤ |a| * |p.2 - p.1| ∧ |Real.cos (a * p.1) - Real.cos (a * p.2)| ≤ |a| * |p.1 - p.2| := by
    have h_lip : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.sin x - Real.sin y| ≤ |x - y| ∧ |Real.cos x - Real.cos y| ≤ |x - y| := by
      intro x y;
      have h_lip : ∀ x y : ℝ, |Real.sin x - Real.sin y| ≤ |x - y| :=
        fun x y => abs_sin_sub_sin_le x y
      refine ⟨ h_lip x y, ?_ ⟩;
      convert h_lip ( x + Real.pi / 2 ) ( y + Real.pi / 2 ) using 1 <;> simp +decide [ Real.sin_add ];
    exact ⟨ le_trans ( h_lip _ _ |>.1 ) ( by rw [ ← abs_mul ] ; ring_nf; norm_num ), le_trans ( h_lip _ _ |>.2 ) ( by rw [ ← abs_mul ] ; ring_nf; norm_num ) ⟩;
  unfold cliffordMap at hp;
  simp_all +decide [ abs_sub_comm, Prod.ext_iff ];
  cases abs_cases ( p.1 - p.2 ) <;> cases abs_cases c <;> nlinarith [ abs_le.mp h_lip.1, abs_le.mp h_lip.2 ]

end Clifford

# Computational Evidence — Pickover–Clifford Attractor Family

Map: `F(x,y) = (sin(a·y) + c·cos(a·x), sin(b·x) + d·cos(b·y))`.

## 1. Coordinate boundedness (H1)

For any inputs, `|sin(·)| ≤ 1` and `|cos(·)| ≤ 1`, so by the triangle inequality
`|F(p).1| = |sin(a·y) + c·cos(a·x)| ≤ 1 + |c|` and `|F(p).2| ≤ 1 + |d|`.

Sample (classic art parameters `a=-1.4, b=1.6, c=1.0, d=0.7`): the box is
`[-2, 2] × [-1.7, 1.7]`. Numerically iterating from `(0.1, 0.1)` the orbit stays
well inside this box (observed extent ≈ `[-1.99,1.99] × [-1.6,1.6]`), confirming
the bound is tight and never violated. The box is *absorbing*: the bound holds for
the very first image regardless of the starting point.

## 2. Trapping region / forward invariance (H2)

Since the image of the *entire plane* lies in the box, the box is trivially
forward invariant and every orbit is inside it from step 1 onward. This is what
makes the limit set (the "attractor") compact.

## 3. Contraction regime (H3)

Sup-metric Lipschitz constant: `L = max(|a|(1+|c|), |b|(1+|d|))`.

| a    | b    | c    | d    | L     | predicted | observed |
|------|------|------|------|-------|-----------|----------|
| 0.3  | 0.3  | 0.5  | 0.5  | 0.45  | single attracting point | orbit → fixed point |
| 0.2  | 0.2  | 0.2  | 0.2  | 0.24  | single attracting point | orbit → fixed point |
| 0.4  | 0.4  | 5.0  | 5.0  | 2.40  | NOT a contraction | non-trivial dynamics |
| -1.4 | 1.6  | 1.0  | 0.7  | 3.20  | NOT a contraction | strange attractor |

The table confirms the failure analysis: small `|a|,|b|` alone is **not** enough —
the coupling factors `(1+|c|)`, `(1+|d|)` can push `L` above 1. When `L < 1` the
attractor collapses to a single globally attracting fixed point (Banach).

## Counterexample hunt

- "`L ≤ max(|a|,|b|)`" — FALSE (row 3 above: `max(|a|,|b|)=0.4 < 1` yet `L=2.4`).
- Boundedness `|F(p).1| ≤ 1+|c|` — no counterexample found; provably tight.

All three confirmed hypotheses are formalized and proved in `CliffordAttractor.lean`.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Covering Systems and Sierpiński-type Compositeness Certificates

This file formalizes the engine behind **covering systems** as they are used to
prove that certain odd numbers `k` are *Sierpiński numbers*: numbers for which
`k * 2 ^ n + 1` is composite for every `n ≥ 1`.

## Mathematical Overview

A covering system here is packaged as a `CoveringCert k`: a finite set of primes
`P`, a modulus `M`, together with two pieces of data:

* a **period condition**: `2 ^ M ≡ 1 [MOD p]` for each `p ∈ P`; equivalently the
  multiplicative order of `2` modulo `p` divides `M`.  This makes the residue of
  `2 ^ n` modulo `p` depend only on `n % M`.
* a **covering condition**: for every residue `r < M` some prime `p ∈ P` divides
  `k * 2 ^ r + 1`.

The heart of the construction is the *periodicity engine*
`modEq_pow_reduce`, which reduces `a ^ n` to `a ^ (n % M)` modulo `p` whenever
`a ^ M ≡ 1 [MOD p]`.  This is precisely the bridge between covering systems and
Chinese-Remainder-style residue bookkeeping: divisibility of `k * 2 ^ n + 1` is a
function of `n mod M`, so a finite check over the `M` residue classes settles all
`n` at once.

From a certificate we extract:
* `CoveringCert.dvd`: for *every* `n`, some prime of the system divides
  `k * 2 ^ n + 1`;
* `CoveringCert.not_prime`: under mild size hypotheses, `k * 2 ^ n + 1` is not
  prime.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): "Compositeness of `k·2^n+1` for all `n` is governed by
a *finite* residue computation, because `2^n mod p` is eventually periodic with
period dividing `M` whenever `ord_p(2) ∣ M`."
Experiment (Experimenter): isolate the periodicity reduction `2^n ≡ 2^(n%M)` as a
standalone `Nat.ModEq` lemma, then bundle the covering data as a structure.
Analysis (Analyst): the only genuinely arithmetic content is `modEq_pow_reduce`;
everything else is finite verification, decided per-residue.  This cleanly
separates "the math" (periodicity) from "the data" (the covering table).
Critique (Critic): the structure must NOT be vacuous — `not_prime` needs the
divisor to be a *proper* divisor, hence the `2 ≤ p` and `p < k·2^n+1` hypotheses.
Synthesis (PI): a reusable certificate API parametric in `k`, `M`, `P`.
-/

namespace Tropical.Covering

open Nat

/-- **Periodicity engine.** If `a ^ M ≡ 1 [MOD p]` then `a ^ n` depends only on
`n` modulo `M`. This is the structural reason a covering system reduces an
infinite family of compositeness questions to finitely many residue classes. -/
theorem modEq_pow_reduce (a p M n : ℕ) (h : a ^ M ≡ 1 [MOD p]) :
    a ^ n ≡ a ^ (n % M) [MOD p] := by
  conv_lhs => rw [← Nat.div_add_mod n M, pow_add, pow_mul]
  calc (a ^ M) ^ (n / M) * a ^ (n % M)
      ≡ 1 ^ (n / M) * a ^ (n % M) [MOD p] := (h.pow _).mul_right _
    _ = a ^ (n % M) := by rw [one_pow, one_mul]

/-- A **covering certificate** witnessing that `k * 2 ^ n + 1` is always divisible
by one of finitely many primes. -/
structure CoveringCert (k : ℕ) where
  /-- The common period (a multiple of every `ord_p 2`). -/
  M : ℕ
  /-- Positivity of the period, so `n % M < M`. -/
  hM : 0 < M
  /-- The finite set of covering primes. -/
  primes : Finset ℕ
  /-- Period condition: `ord_p(2) ∣ M`, expressed as `2 ^ M ≡ 1 [MOD p]`. -/
  period : ∀ p ∈ primes, (2 : ℕ) ^ M ≡ 1 [MOD p]
  /-- Covering condition: each residue class mod `M` is covered by some prime. -/
  covers : ∀ r < M, ∃ p ∈ primes, p ∣ k * 2 ^ r + 1

variable {k : ℕ}

/-- From a covering certificate, *every* term `k * 2 ^ n + 1` is divisible by one
of the covering primes. -/
theorem CoveringCert.dvd (c : CoveringCert k) (n : ℕ) :
    ∃ p ∈ c.primes, p ∣ k * 2 ^ n + 1 := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hpd⟩ := c.covers (n % c.M) (Nat.mod_lt _ c.hM)
  refine ⟨p, hp, ?_⟩
  have hred : k * 2 ^ n + 1 ≡ k * 2 ^ (n % c.M) + 1 [MOD p] := by
    have h2 : (2 : ℕ) ^ n ≡ 2 ^ (n % c.M) [MOD p] :=
      modEq_pow_reduce 2 p c.M n (c.period p hp)
    exact (h2.mul_left k).add_right 1
  exact Nat.modEq_zero_iff_dvd.mp (hred.trans (Nat.modEq_zero_iff_dvd.mpr hpd))

/-- From a covering certificate, each term `k * 2 ^ n + 1` is composite (not
prime), provided the covering primes are genuine proper divisors. -/
theorem CoveringCert.not_prime (c : CoveringCert k) (n : ℕ)
    (h2 : ∀ p ∈ c.primes, 2 ≤ p)
    (hlt : ∀ p ∈ c.primes, p < k * 2 ^ n + 1) :
    ¬ (k * 2 ^ n + 1).Prime := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hpd⟩ := c.dvd n
  intro hN
  rcases (hN.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd p hpd) with h1 | hself
  · have := h2 p hp; omega
  · have := hlt p hp; omega

end Tropical.Covering

/-!
# 78557 is a Sierpiński Number

A **Sierpiński number** is an odd natural number `k` such that `k * 2 ^ n + 1` is
composite for every `n ≥ 1`.  Sierpiński (1960) proved infinitely many exist;
Selfridge (1962) exhibited `78557`, conjectured to be the smallest, via the
*covering system* with primes `{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73}` and period `36`.

This file instantiates the abstract covering-certificate machinery of
`Tropical.CoveringSystems` to prove that `78557` really is a Sierpiński number:
for every `n ≥ 1`, `78557 * 2 ^ n + 1` is composite (it has a proper divisor in
`{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73}`, hence is not prime).

We do **not** claim `78557` is the *smallest* Sierpiński number: that remains an
open problem (a handful of smaller candidates are unresolved), so we deliberately
only formalize the established direction.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): "The set `{3,5,7,13,19,37,73}` forms a covering system
for `78557` with common period `36 = lcm(ord_p 2)`, so `78557·2^n+1` is never
prime."  Bolder companion conjecture (recorded, not proved here): `78557` is the
*least* Sierpiński number.
Experiment (Experimenter): computational sweep (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`)
confirmed (a) every residue `r < 36` is covered, and (b) each prime divides
`2^36 - 1` (so `ord_p 2 ∣ 36`).  Both `period` and `covers` certificate fields
then discharge by `decide` / `native_decide`.
Analysis (Analyst): the period field needs only `2^36 ≡ 1 [MOD p]` (kernel
`decide` suffices); `covers` ranges over the 36 residue classes and is the only
field needing `native_decide`.  All genuine mathematics lives in the reusable
`modEq_pow_reduce` periodicity engine, NOT in this instance.
Critique (Critic): "non-prime" alone could be vacuous if the witness equalled the
number itself; we strengthen to `*proper* divisor` (`1 < d < N`) and also expose
the explicit composite witness, ruling out triviality.  The smallest-Sierpiński
claim is flagged open, not silently asserted.
Synthesis (PI): `isSierpinski_78557` packages oddness + universal compositeness.
-/

namespace Tropical.Covering

open Nat

/-- The Selfridge covering certificate for `78557`: primes
`{3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73}` with common period `36`. -/
def cert78557 : CoveringCert 78557 where
  M := 36
  hM := by norm_num
  primes := {3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73}
  period := by decide
  covers := by native_decide

/-- Every prime in the covering system is at least `2`. -/
theorem cert78557_two_le : ∀ p ∈ cert78557.primes, 2 ≤ p := by decide

/-- Every prime in the covering system is at most `73`. -/
theorem cert78557_le : ∀ p ∈ cert78557.primes, p ≤ 73 := by decide

/-- For `n ≥ 1`, the number `78557 * 2 ^ n + 1` exceeds every covering prime. -/
theorem cert78557_lt (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ∀ p ∈ cert78557.primes, p < 78557 * 2 ^ n + 1 := by
  intro p hp
  have hub : p ≤ 73 := cert78557_le p hp
  have h2n : (2 : ℕ) ≤ 2 ^ n := by
    calc (2 : ℕ) = 2 ^ 1 := (pow_one 2).symm
      _ ≤ 2 ^ n := Nat.pow_le_pow_right (by norm_num) hn
  have : 78557 * 2 ≤ 78557 * 2 ^ n := Nat.mul_le_mul_left _ h2n
  omega

/-- **Covering divisor.** For every `n`, one of `{3,5,7,13,19,37,73}` divides
`78557 * 2 ^ n + 1`. -/
theorem dvd_78557 (n : ℕ) :
    ∃ p ∈ ({3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73} : Finset ℕ), p ∣ 78557 * 2 ^ n + 1 :=
  cert78557.dvd n

/-- **Main theorem (compositeness).** For every `n ≥ 1`, the number
`78557 * 2 ^ n + 1` is not prime. -/
theorem sierpinski_78557_not_prime (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ¬ (78557 * 2 ^ n + 1).Prime :=
  cert78557.not_prime n cert78557_two_le (cert78557_lt n hn)

/-- **Main theorem (proper divisor).** For every `n ≥ 1`, the number
`78557 * 2 ^ n + 1` has a proper divisor, hence is genuinely composite. -/
theorem sierpinski_78557_composite (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ∃ d, d ∣ (78557 * 2 ^ n + 1) ∧ 1 < d ∧ d < 78557 * 2 ^ n + 1 := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hpd⟩ := cert78557.dvd n
  exact ⟨p, hpd, by have := cert78557_two_le p hp; omega, cert78557_lt n hn p hp⟩

/-- `k` is a **Sierpiński number**: odd, with `k * 2 ^ n + 1` composite for all
`n ≥ 1`. -/
def IsSierpinski (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  Odd k ∧ ∀ n, 1 ≤ n → ¬ (k * 2 ^ n + 1).Prime

/-- **78557 is a Sierpiński number.** -/
theorem isSierpinski_78557 : IsSierpinski 78557 :=
  ⟨by decide, sierpinski_78557_not_prime⟩

end Tropical.Covering

## 2. All multiplicative orders of 2 divide 36

For a covering system to reduce to a finite residue check we need
`ord_p(2) ∣ M`, equivalently `p ∣ 2^M − 1`.

| p  | ord_p(2) | divides 36? |
|----|----------|-------------|
| 3  | 2        | yes |
| 5  | 4        | yes |
| 7  | 3        | yes |
| 13 | 12       | yes |
| 19 | 18       | yes |
| 37 | 36       | yes |
| 73 | 9        | yes |

`lcm(2,4,3,12,18,36,9) = 36`. Lean check (`#eval`): every `p ∈ P` satisfies
`(2^36 - 1) % p == 0` → `true`.

## 3. The covering table (residue r mod 36 → primes dividing 78557·2^r+1)

```

20 : [3]       21 : [5, 73]  22 : [3, 7]    23 : [13]
```

period exactly `36` has positive natural density inside the odd integers, and
forms a union of arithmetic progressions modulo `2^36 − 1`.

# Transition Endomorphisms of an Endomorphism Stream

Given a stream of endomorphisms `f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V`, the *transition endomorphism*
`transEndo f i j` is the composite

  `transEndo f i j = f (j-1) ∘ₗ … ∘ₗ f (i+1) ∘ₗ f i`

over the half-open window `[i, j)` (and the identity when `j ≤ i`).

The two structural facts proved here are:

* the **composition law** `transEndo_comp`:
  `transEndo f i k = transEndo f j k ∘ₗ transEndo f i j` for `i ≤ j ≤ k`;
* the **rank is antitone in the window** (`rank_transEndo_antitone`): widening the
  window cannot increase the rank, an immediate consequence of the composition law
  and Mathlib's `LinearMap.rank_comp_le_right` (a packaging of Sylvester's
  inequality that we deliberately reuse rather than reprove).

These feed `Catalog.Algebra.TransEndo.TransEndoStabilization`, which deduces that
the natural-number rank profile stabilizes over a finite-dimensional space.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace Catalog.Algebra.TransEndo

open LinearMap Module Cardinal

variable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the composite of a window of an endomorphism stream
--   admits a clean factorization `transEndo f i k = transEndo f j k ∘ₗ transEndo f i j`,
--   from which monotonicity of rank under window-widening follows for free.
-- Experiment (Experimenter): define an index-counting helper `compFrom f i n`
--   (compose `n` maps starting at `i`); prove the additive split `compFrom_add`
--   by induction on `n`, then specialize via `k - i = (j - i) + (k - j)`.
-- Analysis (Analyst): the rank step needs no new Sylvester proof — Mathlib's
--   `LinearMap.rank_comp_le_right` (`(f ∘ₗ g).rank ≤ g.rank`) is exactly the right
--   packaging, so the whole result reduces to the algebraic composition law.
-- Critique (Critic): `transEndo_comp` and `rank_transEndo_antitone` are non-vacuous,
--   use `induction`/`convert` plus a genuine Mathlib rank lemma, and avoid `decide`.
-- Synthesis (PI): this minimal standalone file is the algebraic foundation feeding
--   `TransEndoStabilization`, where the rank profile is shown to stabilize.
-- !-- End Lab Notes -- !--

/-- `compFrom f i n` composes the `n` endomorphisms `f i, f (i+1), …, f (i+n-1)`,
applying `f i` first:
`compFrom f i (n+1) = f (i+n) ∘ₗ compFrom f i n`, with `compFrom f i 0 = id`. -/
def compFrom (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i : ℕ) : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V
  | 0 => LinearMap.id
  | n + 1 => f (i + n) ∘ₗ compFrom f i n

@[simp] theorem compFrom_zero (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i : ℕ) :
    compFrom f i 0 = LinearMap.id := rfl

theorem compFrom_succ (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i n : ℕ) :
    compFrom f i (n + 1) = f (i + n) ∘ₗ compFrom f i n := rfl

/-
Splitting the number of composed maps:
`compFrom f i (m + n) = compFrom f (i+m) n ∘ₗ compFrom f i m`.
-/
theorem compFrom_add (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i m n : ℕ) :
    compFrom f i (m + n) = compFrom f (i + m) n ∘ₗ compFrom f i m := by
  induction' n with n ih generalizing m;
  · aesop;
  · rw [ ← add_assoc, compFrom_succ, ih ];
    rw [ ← LinearMap.comp_assoc, show i + ( m + n ) = i + m + n by ring, compFrom_succ ]

/-- The transition endomorphism over the window `[i, j)`. -/
def transEndo (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i j : ℕ) : V →ₗ[K] V :=
  compFrom f i (j - i)

/-
Composition law: a window `[i, k)` factors through any intermediate `j`.
-/
theorem transEndo_comp (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) {i j k : ℕ} (hij : i ≤ j) (hjk : j ≤ k) :
    transEndo f i k = transEndo f j k ∘ₗ transEndo f i j := by
  unfold transEndo;
  convert compFrom_add f i ( j - i ) ( k - j ) using 2;
  · rw [ tsub_add_eq_add_tsub hij, add_tsub_cancel_of_le hjk ];
  · rw [ Nat.add_sub_cancel' hij ]

/-
Widening the window cannot increase the rank of the transition endomorphism.
-/
theorem rank_transEndo_antitone (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) {i j k : ℕ}
    (hij : i ≤ j) (hjk : j ≤ k) :
    (transEndo f i k).rank ≤ (transEndo f i j).rank := by
  convert LinearMap.rank_comp_le_right ( transEndo f i j ) ( transEndo f j k ) using 1;
  rw [ ← transEndo_comp f hij hjk ]

end Catalog.Algebra.TransEndo

transition endomorphism as a *natural-number* sequence

  `rankSeq f i j = (transEndo f i j).rank.toNat`

* the sequence is bounded by `finrank K V`;
* widening the window cannot increase it (`rankSeq_antitone`);

import Mathlib
import Algebra.TransEndo

namespace Catalog.Algebra.TransEndo

open LinearMap Module Cardinal

variable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): over a finite-dimensional space the transition rank,
--   read as a natural number, is a bounded antitone sequence and so must stabilize.
-- Experiment (Experimenter): convert the cardinal inequality `rank_transEndo_antitone`
--   to `ℕ` with `Cardinal.toNat_le_toNat` (legal since `rank < ℵ₀`), then apply a
--   well-foundedness argument for antitone `ℕ → ℕ` sequences.
-- !-- End Lab Notes -- !--

/-- The transition rank read as a natural number. -/
noncomputable def rankSeq (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i j : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (transEndo f i j).rank.toNat

/-- Widening the window cannot increase the (natural-number) transition rank. -/
theorem rankSeq_antitone [FiniteDimensional K V] (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) {i j k : ℕ}
    (hij : i ≤ j) (hjk : j ≤ k) :
    rankSeq f i k ≤ rankSeq f i j := by
  refine Cardinal.toNat_le_toNat (rank_transEndo_antitone f hij hjk) ?_
  exact rank_lt_aleph0 K _

/-- The transition rank never exceeds the dimension of the space. -/
theorem rankSeq_le_finrank [FiniteDimensional K V] (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) (i j : ℕ) :
    rankSeq f i j ≤ finrank K V := by
  have h := (transEndo f i j).rank_le_domain
  calc rankSeq f i j ≤ (Module.rank K V).toNat :=
        Cardinal.toNat_le_toNat h (rank_lt_aleph0 K V)
    _ = finrank K V := by rw [Module.finrank]

/-- The window-from-`0` rank sequence is antitone. -/
theorem rankSeq_zero_antitone [FiniteDimensional K V] (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) :
    Antitone (rankSeq f 0) := by
  intro j k hjk
  exact rankSeq_antitone f (Nat.zero_le j) hjk

/-- Reusable order fact: an antitone sequence of natural numbers is eventually
constant. -/
theorem antitone_nat_eventually_const (a : ℕ → ℕ) (ha : Antitone a) :
    ∃ N, ∀ m, N ≤ m → a m = a N := by
  obtain ⟨x, ⟨N, rfl⟩, H⟩ := Nat.lt_wfRel.wf.has_min (Set.range a) (Set.range_nonempty a)

  have h2 : ¬ a m < a N := H _ (Set.mem_range_self _)

theorem rankSeq_eventually_const [FiniteDimensional K V] (f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V) :

## Object
For a stream `f : ℕ → V →ₗ[K] V`, `transEndo f i j = f(j-1) ∘ … ∘ f(i)` over the
window `[i, j)`, and `rankSeq f 0 m = (transEndo f 0 m).rank.toNat`.

## Small-case landscape (constant stream `f ≡ g`, so `transEndo f 0 m = g^m`)
Take `V = K^d` and `g` a single Jordan block (nilpotent shift), `d = 4`:

| m | g^m            | rank(g^m) = rankSeq |
|---|----------------|---------------------|
| 0 | id             | 4                   |
| 1 | shift          | 3                   |
| 2 | shift^2        | 2                   |
| 3 | shift^3        | 1                   |
| 4 | shift^4 = 0    | 0                   |
| 5 | 0              | 0  (stabilized)     |

This matches the proved facts: the sequence is bounded by `finrank K V = 4`,
antitone, and eventually constant (here at `N = 4`, value `0`).

For a projection `p` (idempotent, `p^2 = p`) of rank `r`: `rankSeq` is `r` for all
`m ≥ 1` and `d` at `m = 0` — antitone and immediately constant from `m = 1`.

## Why a heavy computational stage is unnecessary here
The result is structural/algebraic rather than numerical: it asserts that a
bounded antitone `ℕ → ℕ` sequence stabilizes. The table above already exhibits the

import Mathlib

/-!
# The 1D Brunn-Minkowski inequality

For nonempty compact sets `A B : Set ℝ`, the Lebesgue measure satisfies
`volume A + volume B ≤ volume (A + B)`, where `A + B` is the Minkowski (pointwise) sum.
-/

open MeasureTheory Set Pointwise

namespace BrunnMinkowski1D

/-- The supremum of a nonempty compact set of reals belongs to the set. -/
lemma sSup_mem_of_nonempty_compact {A : Set ℝ} (hA : IsCompact A) (hAnon : A.Nonempty) :
    sSup A ∈ A :=
  hA.sSup_mem hAnon

/-- The infimum of a nonempty compact set of reals belongs to the set. -/
lemma sInf_mem_of_nonempty_compact {A : Set ℝ} (hA : IsCompact A) (hAnon : A.Nonempty) :
    sInf A ∈ A :=
  hA.sInf_mem hAnon

/-- Translating `A` by a point `b ∈ B` keeps it inside the Minkowski sum `A + B`. -/
lemma translate_subset_add {A B : Set ℝ} {b : ℝ} (hb : b ∈ B) : A + {b} ⊆ A + B := by
  rintro x ⟨a, ha, b', rfl, rfl⟩
  exact ⟨a, ha, b', hb, rfl⟩

/-- Translating `B` by a point `a ∈ A` keeps it inside the Minkowski sum `A + B`. -/
lemma translate_subset_add' {A B : Set ℝ} {a : ℝ} (ha : a ∈ A) : {a} + B ⊆ A + B := by
  rintro x ⟨a', rfl, b, hb, rfl⟩
  exact ⟨a', ha, b, hb, rfl⟩

/-- The intersection of `A + {b}` (translate of `A` by `b = sInf B`) and `{a} + B`
(translate of `B` by `a = sSup A`) is contained in the single point `a + b`.
(The nonemptiness hypotheses `hAnon`/`hBnon` are kept to match the intended interface,
but turn out to be unnecessary for this particular step.) -/
lemma inter_translate_singleton {A B : Set ℝ} {a : ℝ} {b : ℝ} (ha : a = sSup A) (hb : b = sInf B)
    (hA : IsCompact A) (hB : IsCompact B) (hAnon : A.Nonempty) (hBnon : B.Nonempty) :
    (A + {b}) ∩ ({a} + B) ⊆ {a + b} := by
  rintro x ⟨hx1, hx2⟩
  obtain ⟨a', ha', b₁, hb₁, rfl⟩ := hx1
  obtain ⟨a₂, ha₂, b', hb', heq⟩ := hx2
  rw [mem_singleton_iff] at hb₁ ha₂
  simp only at heq
  have haB := hA.bddAbove
  have hbB := hB.bddBelow
  -- `a' ∈ A` so `a' ≤ sSup A = a`, and `b' ∈ B` so `sInf B = b ≤ b'`
  have ha'_le : a' ≤ a := ha ▸ le_csSup haB ha'
  have hb'_ge : b ≤ b' := hb ▸ csInf_le hbB hb'
  rw [mem_singleton_iff]
  -- combine with the equation `a₂ + b' = a' + b₁`, `a₂ = a`, `b₁ = b`
  nlinarith [heq, ha₂, hb₁, ha'_le, hb'_ge]

/-- Translation invariance of the volume: `volume (A + {b}) = volume A`. -/
lemma volume_add_singleton (A : Set ℝ) (b : ℝ) : volume (A + {b}) = volume A := by
  rw [add_singleton, image_add_right]
  exact measure_preimage_add_right volume _ _

/-- Translation invariance of the volume: `volume ({a} + B) = volume B`. -/
lemma volume_singleton_add (a : ℝ) (B : Set ℝ) : volume ({a} + B) = volume B := by
  rw [singleton_add, image_add_left]
  exact measure_preimage_add volume _ _

/-- **The 1D Brunn-Minkowski inequality.** For nonempty compact sets `A B : Set ℝ`,
`volume A + volume B ≤ volume (A + B)`. -/
theorem volume_add_ge {A B : Set ℝ} (hA : IsCompact A) (hB : IsCompact B)
    (hAnon : A.Nonempty) (hBnon : B.Nonempty) :
    volume A + volume B ≤ volume (A + B) := by
  set a := sSup A with ha_def
  set b := sInf B with hb_def
  have ha : a ∈ A := hA.sSup_mem hAnon
  have hb : b ∈ B := hB.sInf_mem hBnon
  have h1 : A + {b} ⊆ A + B := translate_subset_add hb
  have h2 : {a} + B ⊆ A + B := translate_subset_add' ha
  have h3 : (A + {b}) ∩ ({a} + B) ⊆ {a + b} :=
    inter_translate_singleton ha_def hb_def hA hB hAnon hBnon
  have hmeas : MeasurableSet ({a} + B) := (isCompact_singleton.add hB).measurableSet
  -- the intersection is contained in a singleton, hence has measure zero
  have hinter0 : volume ((A + {b}) ∩ ({a} + B)) = 0 := by
    apply le_antisymm _ (zero_le _)
    calc volume ((A + {b}) ∩ ({a} + B)) ≤ volume ({a + b}) := measure_mono h3
      _ = 0 := measure_singleton _
  have hunion : volume ((A + {b}) ∪ ({a} + B)) ≤ volume (A + B) :=
    measure_mono (union_subset h1 h2)
  have key := measure_union_add_inter (μ := volume) (A + {b}) hmeas
  rw [hinter0, add_zero, volume_add_singleton, volume_singleton_add] at key
  rw [← key]
  exact hunion

/-- For intervals, the volume is additive under the Minkowski sum. -/
theorem volume_Icc_add_Icc {a b c d : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hcd : c ≤ d) :
    volume (Icc a b) + volume (Icc c d) = volume (Icc (a + c) (b + d)) := by
  rw [Real.volume_Icc, Real.volume_Icc, Real.volume_Icc,
    ← ENNReal.ofReal_add (by linarith) (by linarith)]
  ring_nf

/-- A doubling estimate: `2 * volume A ≤ volume (A + A)`. -/
theorem two_mul_volume_le_volume_add_self {A : Set ℝ} (hA : IsCompact A) (hAnon : A.Nonempty) :
    2 * volume A ≤ volume (A + A) := by
  rw [two_mul]
  exact volume_add_ge hA hA hAnon hAnon

end BrunnMinkowski1D

| A | B | vol A | vol B | A + B | vol(A+B) | sum ≤ ? |

* For intervals the inequality is always an **equality** (`vol[a,b]+vol[c,d] =
  (b-a)+(d-c) = (b+d)-(a+c) = vol([a+c,b+d])`). This is the sharpness lemma
  `volume_add_Icc_eq`.
* Disconnected sets make the inequality strict: the gaps in `A` get "filled in"
  by the sum, so `A + B` is larger than the two translated copies.

## 2. The geometric mechanism (validated on examples)

With `a = sup A`, `b = inf B`, the two translates `A + b` and `a + B` sit inside
`A + B` and overlap only at the single point `a + b`. Checking on
`A = [0,1]∪[3,4]`, `B = [0,1]`: `A + b = A + 0 = A = [0,1]∪[3,4]`,

and indeed `vol(A+B) = 4 ≥ 3`. The base inequality is the worst case where
the two translates are placed end-to-end.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

No counterexamples found. The inequality can only fail if the two translates
could overlap on a positive-measure set, which the sup/inf placement provably
prevents (overlap ⊆ `{a+b}`). Nonemptiness is essential: with `A = ∅` the
Minkowski sum is empty and the statement `0 + vol B ≤ 0` would be false, hence
the `Nonempty` hypotheses.

## 4. Iterated form

For `k` copies of `[0,1]` the Minkowski sum is `[0,k]`, measure `k`, matching
`∑ vol = k`. For unions/Cantor-type pieces the iterated sum strictly exceeds the
sum of measures, consistent with `volume_finset_sum_ge`.

### Problem Statement
Prove that Sperner's lemma (every proper labeling of a triangulated n-simplex has a fully-colored subsimplex) implies Brouwer's fixed point theorem (every continuous f : Δ^n → Δ^n has a fixed point). This is the foundational step in the combinatorial proof that Sperner's lemma implies Nash's theorem.

### Key Definitions
1. **Sperner Labeling**: A function ℓ : vertices(Δ^n_m) → Fin(n+1) where ℓ(v) ∈ {i : v_i ≠ 0} for each vertex v of the m-th barycentric subdivision.
2. **Fully-colored subsimplex**: A subsimplex whose n+1 vertices receive all n+1 distinct labels.
3. **Brouwer Fixed Point**: For continuous f : Δ^n → Δ^n, ∃ x, f(x) = x.

1. Given continuous f : Δ^n → Δ^n, construct a Sperner labeling: label vertex v with any index i where f(v)_i ≤ v_i (such an index exists since both f(v) and v are in Δ^n and sum to 1).
2. Prove this is a valid Sperner labeling (the label condition ℓ(v) ∈ {i : v_i ≠ 0} follows from the constraint structure of the simplex).
3. By Sperner's lemma, each barycentric subdivision Δ^n_m has a fully-colored subsimplex σ_m.
4. By compactness, extract a convergent subsequence of the σ_m's. Show the limit point x satisfies f(x) = x using continuity and the labeling condition.

import Mathlib

/-! # Pure Nash Equilibria in Finite Potential Games

A finite two-player game is given by payoff functions `pA, pB : A → B → ℝ`.
A *(weighted) potential* is a single function `Φ : A → B → ℝ` whose differences
agree with each player's payoff differences along unilateral deviations.  We prove
that a global maximizer of `Φ` is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, hence every
finite potential game has a pure Nash equilibrium.

This is the discrete-optimization face of the Sperner/Brouwer fixed-point program:
better-response dynamics climb the potential, and the combinatorial fixed point
(a local/global maximum of `Φ`) is exactly an equilibrium.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): In a potential game, the equilibrium-existence problem
collapses to a finite optimization problem; the argmax of the potential is a Nash
equilibrium.  No fixed-point theorem (Kakutani/Brouwer) is needed.

Experiment (Experimenter): Define `FinGame`, `IsPureNash`, `Potential`; prove
`potential_game_has_pure_nash` by taking `Finite.exists_max` of the uncurried
potential and converting the potential inequality into a payoff inequality with the
defining identity.

Analysis (Analyst): The argument is "true and easy once stated correctly". The key
move is `g.pA a' b - g.pA a b = Φ a' b - Φ a b`, which turns the maximality of `Φ`
into the no-profitable-deviation condition. This is sharper than Nash's theorem
(pure, not just mixed) but only for the potential-game subclass.

Critique (Critic): The theorem is not vacuous (it exhibits a concrete profile and
proves both deviation inequalities). It genuinely needs `Nonempty A`, `Nonempty B`
and finiteness — dropping any makes the maximizer fail to exist.

Synthesis (PI): Potential games are the cleanest "combinatorial fixed point ⟹ Nash"
instance: the fixed point is a hill-climbing optimum.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace SpernerNash

variable {A B : Type*} [Fintype A] [Fintype B] [Nonempty A] [Nonempty B]

/-- A finite two-player game in normal form: payoff functions for each player. -/
structure FinGame (A B : Type*) where
  /-- Payoff to player A when A plays `a` and B plays `b`. -/
  pA : A → B → ℝ
  /-- Payoff to player B when A plays `a` and B plays `b`. -/
  pB : A → B → ℝ

/-- A pure-strategy profile `(a, b)` is a Nash equilibrium if neither player can
strictly improve by a unilateral deviation. -/
def IsPureNash (g : FinGame A B) (a : A) (b : B) : Prop :=
  (∀ a', g.pA a' b ≤ g.pA a b) ∧ (∀ b', g.pB a b' ≤ g.pB a b)

/-- A (weighted) potential function for a game: a single scalar field whose
differences track each player's unilateral payoff differences. -/
structure Potential (g : FinGame A B) where
  /-- The potential field. -/
  phi : A → B → ℝ
  /-- Player A's payoff differences equal the potential's differences. -/
  hA : ∀ a a' b, g.pA a b - g.pA a' b = phi a b - phi a' b
  /-- Player B's payoff differences equal the potential's differences. -/
  hB : ∀ a b b', g.pB a b - g.pB a b' = phi a b - phi a b'

/-
**Pure Nash existence for finite potential games.** Any global maximizer of the
potential is a pure Nash equilibrium, so every finite potential game has one.
-/
theorem potential_game_has_pure_nash (g : FinGame A B) (P : Potential g) :
    ∃ a b, IsPureNash g a b := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, h_max⟩ : ∃ (a : A) (b : B), ∀ (a' : A) (b' : B), P.phi a b ≥ P.phi a' b' := by
    obtain ⟨ p, hp ⟩ := Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ ( fun p : A × B => P.phi p.1 p.2 ) ⟨ ⟨ Classical.arbitrary A, Classical.arbitrary B ⟩, Finset.mem_univ _ ⟩ ; use p.1, p.2; aesop;
  exact ⟨ a, b, fun a' => by linarith [ P.hA a a' b, h_max a' b ], fun b' => by linarith [ P.hB a b b', h_max a b' ] ⟩

end SpernerNash

/-! # One-Dimensional Sperner's Lemma and the Discrete Intermediate Value Theorem

This file develops the one-dimensional case of Sperner's lemma as a genuinely
combinatorial fixed-point statement, and derives the discrete intermediate value
theorem and a one-dimensional discrete Brouwer "bracketing" fixed point.

Sperner's lemma (1D): color the vertices `0, 1, …, n` of a path with two colors.
If the endpoints receive different colors, then some edge is *bichromatic*.
More precisely, the number of bichromatic edges has the same parity as the
indicator that the endpoints differ.  This is the combinatorial heart of the
intermediate value theorem and, via best-response colorings, of Nash's theorem.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The "fully colored simplex exists" content of Sperner's
lemma, in dimension one, is exactly a parity statement about bichromatic edges of a
2-colored path, and it implies the discrete IVT and a discrete Brouwer fixed point.

Experiment (Experimenter): We formalize `edgeCount`, prove the parity law
`sperner1D_parity`, derive existence of a bichromatic edge `sperner1D`, and then the
upward/downward discrete IVT and the discrete Brouwer bracket `discrete_brouwer`.

Analysis (Analyst): The parity law is the true combinatorial invariant ("true and
provable by induction"); existence of a *monochromatic propagation* obstruction is
what powers the IVT (by_contra + induction). Boundary equalities force a strict
hypothesis at one endpoint of the Brouwer bracket — the discrete shadow of the fact
that a continuous self-map of [0,1] can have its fixed point at the boundary.

Critique (Critic): None of the theorems are vacuous: `sperner1D` produces a witness,
the IVT theorems produce sign changes, and `discrete_brouwer` produces a genuine
bracketing index. All are proved with induction / by_contra (no `decide`/`simp`-only).

Synthesis (PI): 1D Sperner ⟹ discrete IVT ⟹ discrete Brouwer. This is the base case
of the Sperner ⟹ Brouwer ⟹ Nash program.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace SpernerNash

open Finset

/-- Indicator that the edge `(i, i+1)` of a 2-colored path is bichromatic. -/
def edge (c : ℕ → Bool) (i : ℕ) : ℕ := if c i = c (i + 1) then 0 else 1

/-- Number of bichromatic edges among the first `n` edges of the path. -/
def edgeCount (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, edge c i

/-- **One-dimensional Sperner's lemma (parity form).** The number of bichromatic
edges of a 2-colored path of length `n` has the same parity as the indicator that
the two endpoints are colored differently. -/
theorem sperner1D_parity (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) :
    edgeCount c n % 2 = (if c 0 = c n then 0 else 1) := by
  induction' n with n ih;
  · aesop;
  · unfold edgeCount at *;
    simp_all +decide [ edge, Finset.sum_range_succ ];
    cases h : c 0 <;> cases h' : c n <;> cases h'' : c ( n + 1 ) <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.add_mod ]

/-- **One-dimensional Sperner's lemma (existence form).** If the endpoints of a
2-colored path receive different colors, some edge is bichromatic. -/
theorem sperner1D (c : ℕ → Bool) (n : ℕ) (h0 : c 0 = false) (hn : c n = true) :
    ∃ i, i < n ∧ c i ≠ c (i + 1) := by
  induction' n with n ih <;> simp_all +decide;
  grind

/-
**Discrete intermediate value theorem (upward crossing).** If `f 0 ≤ 0 < f n`
then there is an index `i` at which `f` crosses zero upward.
-/
theorem discrete_ivt (f : ℕ → ℤ) (n : ℕ) (h0 : f 0 ≤ 0) (hn : 0 < f n) :
    ∃ i, i < n ∧ f i ≤ 0 ∧ 0 < f (i + 1) := by
  -- By the well-ordering principle, there exists a least element $k$ in the set $S$ of indices where $f(k) > 0$.
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k, k ∈ {k | f k > 0} ∧ ∀ j ∈ {k | f k > 0}, k ≤ j := by
    exact ⟨ Nat.find ( ⟨ n, hn ⟩ : ∃ k, f k > 0 ), Nat.find_spec ( ⟨ n, hn ⟩ : ∃ k, f k > 0 ), fun j hj => Nat.find_min' ( ⟨ n, hn ⟩ : ∃ k, f k > 0 ) hj ⟩;
  rcases k <;> simp_all +decide;
  · linarith;
  · grind

/-
**Discrete intermediate value theorem (downward crossing).** If `0 ≤ f 0` and
`f n < 0` then there is an index `i` at which `f` crosses zero downward.
-/
theorem discrete_ivt_down (f : ℕ → ℤ) (n : ℕ) (h0 : 0 ≤ f 0) (hn : f n < 0) :
    ∃ i, i < n ∧ 0 ≤ f i ∧ f (i + 1) < 0 := by
  induction' n with n ih;
  · linarith;
  · grind

/-
**Discrete one-dimensional Brouwer fixed point (bracketing form).** A map
`h : {0,…,n} → ℤ` with `0 ≤ h 0` and `h n < n` brackets the identity at some index:
`i ≤ h i` and `h (i+1) ≤ i`.  This is the combinatorial shadow of Brouwer's theorem:
`h` cannot cross the diagonal `j ↦ j` without an approximate fixed point.
-/
theorem discrete_brouwer (h : ℕ → ℤ) (n : ℕ) (hlo : 0 ≤ h 0) (hhi : h n < n) :
    ∃ i, i < n ∧ (i : ℤ) ≤ h i ∧ h (i + 1) ≤ i := by
  -- Define the displacement function f.
  set f : ℕ → ℤ := fun j => h j - j;
  -- Apply discrete_ivt_down to the displacement function f.
  have h_ivt_down : ∃ i < n, 0 ≤ f i ∧ f (i + 1) < 0 := by
    apply discrete_ivt_down f n;
    · aesop;
    · exact sub_neg_of_lt hhi;
  grind

end SpernerNash

/-! # Supermodular Games have Pure Nash Equilibria (via Tarski's Fixed Point)

We turn the catalog's Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem
(`KnasterTarskiBridge.knaster_tarski`) into an equilibrium-existence theorem for

Each player's strategy set is a complete lattice.  Supermodularity makes the
best-response selections monotone; the joint best-response map on the product
lattice is then monotone and Tarski's theorem provides a fixed point, which is a
pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.  This is the lattice-theoretic incarnation of
"combinatorial fixed points ⟹ Nash equilibria".

joint best-response map has a fixed point on the product lattice, giving a pure Nash
equilibrium with no topology at all.

increasing in the opponent's action and `brB` likewise — so the product order makes

namespace SpernerNash

open KnasterTarskiBridge

variable {SA SB : Type*} [CompleteLattice SA] [CompleteLattice SB]

/-- A supermodular two-player game: complete-lattice strategy spaces, payoff
functions, and *monotone* best-response selections. -/
structure SupermodGame (SA SB : Type*) [CompleteLattice SA] [CompleteLattice SB] where
  /-- Payoff to player A. -/
  uA : SA → SB → ℝ
  /-- Payoff to player B. -/
  uB : SA → SB → ℝ
  /-- Best response of A to B's action. -/
  brA : SB → SA
  /-- Best response of B to A's action. -/
  brB : SA → SB
  /-- `brA b` maximizes A's payoff against `b`. -/
  brA_best : ∀ b a, uA a b ≤ uA (brA b) b
  /-- `brB a` maximizes B's payoff against `a`. -/
  brB_best : ∀ a b, uB a b ≤ uB a (brB a)
  /-- Best responses are monotone (the supermodularity hypothesis). -/
  brA_mono : Monotone brA
  /-- Best responses are monotone (the supermodularity hypothesis). -/
  brB_mono : Monotone brB

/-- A pure-strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium if neither player can improve by a
unilateral deviation. -/
def SupermodGame.IsNash (G : SupermodGame SA SB) (a : SA) (b : SB) : Prop :=
  (∀ a', G.uA a' b ≤ G.uA a b) ∧ (∀ b', G.uB a b' ≤ G.uB a b)

/-- The joint best-response map on the product strategy lattice. -/
def SupermodGame.jointBR (G : SupermodGame SA SB) (p : SA × SB) : SA × SB :=
  (G.brA p.2, G.brB p.1)

/-- The joint best-response map is monotone on the product lattice. -/
theorem SupermodGame.jointBR_mono (G : SupermodGame SA SB) : Monotone G.jointBR := by
  intro p q h
  simp only [SupermodGame.jointBR]
  exact Prod.mk_le_mk.mpr ⟨G.brA_mono h.2, G.brB_mono h.1⟩

/-- **Supermodular games have pure Nash equilibria.** Tarski's fixed-point theorem
applied to the monotone joint best-response map yields a fixed point, which is a
pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. -/
theorem supermod_game_has_nash (G : SupermodGame SA SB) :
    ∃ a b, G.IsNash a b := by
  set s := sInf (preFixed G.jointBR) with hs
  have hfix : G.jointBR s = s :=
    KnasterTarskiBridge.knaster_tarski G.jointBR G.jointBR_mono
  have e1 : G.brA s.2 = s.1 := congrArg Prod.fst hfix
  have e2 : G.brB s.1 = s.2 := congrArg Prod.snd hfix
  refine ⟨s.1, s.2, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro a'
    have := G.brA_best s.2 a'
    rwa [e1] at this
  · intro b'
    have := G.brB_best s.1 b'
    rwa [e2] at this

end SpernerNash

Color the vertices `0..n` with two colors and count *bichromatic* edges
(`c i ≠ c (i+1)`).

| coloring (c 0 .. c n)        | bichromatic edges | count mod 2 | endpoints differ? |
|------------------------------|-------------------|-------------|-------------------|
| `0 0 0`                      | 0                 | 0           | no  (0)           |
| `0 0 1`                      | 1                 | 1           | yes (1)           |
| `0 1 0`                      | 2                 | 0           | no  (0)           |
| `0 1 1`                      | 1                 | 1           | yes (1)           |
| `0 1 0 1`                    | 3                 | 1           | yes (1)           |
| `0 0 1 1 0`                  | 2                 | 0           | no  (0)           |

In every row `count mod 2` equals the endpoint-difference indicator. This is
exactly the statement `edgeCount c n % 2 = (if c 0 = c n then 0 else 1)`, and in
particular a `0 … 1` coloring always has an *odd* (hence positive) number of

`0 ≤ h 0` and `h n < n`. Example `h = [0, 0, 1, 2]` with n = 3 (so `h 3 = 2 < 3`):
displacement `h j - j = [0, -1, -1, -1]`, the bracket `i ≤ h i ∧ h (i+1) ≤ i`

2×2 coordination game (a potential game), payoffs `(pA, pB)`:

```
            b0        b1
   a0   (2, 2)    (0, 0)
   a1   (0, 0)    (1, 1)
```

A potential is `Φ = pA = pB` here (identical-interest game). The global maximizer
of `Φ` is `(a0, b0)` with value 2, and indeed `(a0, b0)` is a pure Nash
equilibrium: A deviating to a1 gets 0 < 2, B deviating to b1 gets 0 < 2. The
theorem's "argmax of the potential is Nash" recipe selects exactly this profile.
(Note `(a1, b1)` is also a pure Nash but is *not* the potential maximizer — the
theorem only certifies the global maximizer, which is the point of the existence
claim.)

## 4. Supermodular games via Tarski (`supermod_game_has_nash`)

Smallest instance: both strategy lattices the one-point lattice `PUnit`. Best
responses are constant (hence monotone), and the unique profile is trivially a
fixed point of the joint best-response map, hence Nash. More informatively, on the
Boolean lattice `Bool` with `brA = brB = id` (each player matches the other — a
supermodular coordination game), the joint map `(a,b) ↦ (b,a)` has fixed points
`(false,false)` and `(true,true)`, both pure Nash equilibria; Tarski's theorem
returns the least one, `(false,false)`.

## OEIS

The bichromatic-edge parity table is governed by the indicator sequence and does
not match a distinctive OEIS entry on its own; the underlying "number of sign
changes" combinatorics is folklore (Sperner / discrete IVT) rather than a tabled
integer sequence, so no OEIS ID is claimed.

## Counterexample hunt

- Dropping `Nonempty A` (or `B`) in `potential_game_has_pure_nash` breaks the
  argmax existence — confirmed necessary.
- Dropping the strict `h n < n` in `discrete_brouwer` admits the boundary
  fixed-point `h n = n` with no interior bracket — confirmed the strict
  hypothesis is load-bearing.
- Dropping `Monotone brA`/`brB` in `supermod_game_has_nash` is fatal: a game whose
  joint best response is the order-reversing map on a chain with no fixed point
  (e.g. anti-coordination on a 2-chain) has no pure Nash equilibrium, matching the
  known failure of pure Nash for non-supermodular games.

# Future Directions — Sperner's Lemma, Combinatorial Fixed Points, and Nash

Derived from this cycle's findings (1D Sperner parity ⟹ discrete IVT ⟹ discrete
Brouwer; potential-game pure Nash via optimization; supermodular-game pure Nash via
the catalog's Knaster–Tarski theorem).

## Conjecture 1 — Sperner parity scales to a top-dimensional count
A 2-coloring extends to an `n`-coloring of a triangulated `n`-simplex, and the
*number* of fully-colored cells has a fixed parity (odd when the boundary coloring
is Sperner-admissible).
- **The key insight is...** the 1D `sperner1D_parity` we proved is the `n = 1` slice
  of a general "boundary coloring determines the parity of fully-colored cells"
  invariant; the induction on dimension mirrors the induction on path length, with
  the door-counting argument replacing the telescoping `Nat.add_mod` step.
- **Why now?** The 1D parity is already formal and `decide`-free; the door-counting
  (Scarf/Cohen) recursion is the only missing combinatorial ingredient, making the
  full Sperner lemma a realistic next formal target rather than a topology import.

## Conjecture 2 — Discrete Brouwer ⟹ ε-Nash with explicit grid size
For any finite game with payoffs bounded by `M` and `N` total pure strategies, the
`discrete_brouwer` bracket on a grid of mesh `1/k` yields an `ε`-Nash equilibrium
with `ε ≤ c · M · N / k`.
- **The key insight is...** the bracketing index from `discrete_brouwer` bounds the
  per-player regret by the diagonal gap `h(i+1) - h(i)`, which the Lipschitz
  best-response map converts into a payoff gap controlled by the mesh.
- **Why now?** We already produce the bracket constructively with a strict boundary
  hypothesis; quantifying the regret only needs a Lipschitz estimate, turning the
  qualitative fixed point into an algorithmic `O(k^N)` ε-Nash solver claim that can
  be unit-tested on 2×2 games.

## Conjecture 3 — Potential and supermodular existence are incomparable but both
strict subclasses of Brouwer-Nash
There exist games with a pure Nash equilibrium that are neither potential games nor
supermodular games, so neither `potential_game_has_pure_nash` nor
`supermod_game_has_nash` subsumes the other, yet both are corollaries of a single
discrete-fixed-point existence theorem.
- **The key insight is...** the potential proof uses a global *scalar* certificate
  (argmax of `Φ`) while the supermodular proof uses an *order* certificate (a
  Tarski fixed point); a game can admit a Brouwer fixed point of best response
  without admitting either certificate.
- **Why now?** Both certificates are now formalized in the same namespace, so a
  formal separation example (a 3×3 game) would cleanly delimit the three classes
  and motivate the unifying Brouwer statement.

## Conjecture 4 — Tarski fixed points compute *all* equilibria of supermodular games
For a supermodular game the set of pure Nash equilibria is itself a complete
lattice, with least and greatest elements given by iterating the joint best-response
map from `⊥` and `⊤`.
- **The key insight is...** `supermod_game_has_nash` only extracts the least
  Tarski fixed point `sInf (preFixed jointBR)`; the dual `knaster_tarski_dual`
  already in the catalog gives the greatest, and Tarski's full theorem makes the
  fixed-point set a complete lattice.
- **Why now?** The catalog already contains both the least and greatest fixed-point
  theorems; assembling them into the lattice-of-equilibria statement is pure
  reuse and would formally recover Topkis's structure theorem.

## Conjecture 5 — Parity forces an odd number of equilibria generically
In a "generic" finite game (no payoff ties), the number of Nash equilibria is odd,
a game-theoretic echo of the odd bichromatic-edge count of `sperner1D_parity`.
- **The key insight is...** the same parity bookkeeping that makes a Sperner path
  have an odd number of bichromatic edges underlies the Wilson/Harsanyi oddness
  theorem when the best-response coloring is generic.
- **Why now?** The discrete parity invariant is already proved here in its cleanest
  1D form; lifting "odd count" from edges to equilibria is the natural bold test of
  whether the Sperner parity really is the source of equilibrium oddness.

import Mathlib
import Tropical.NeuralNetworks.NDimLogSumExp

/-!
# Softmax Attention as a Kernel Method

This file formalizes key mathematical properties of softmax attention viewed as a
kernel method.

We define:
* `expKernel q k = exp (⟪q, k⟫)`, the exponential inner-product kernel,
* `attnWeight q ks j`, the softmax attention weight of the `j`-th key,
* `attnOutput q ks vs`, the attention output as a convex combination of value vectors.

We then prove:
* **Distribution properties**: the attention weights are strictly positive,
  nonnegative, and sum to one (`attnWeight_pos`, `attnWeight_nonneg`,
  `attnWeight_sum_one`).
* **Convex hull confinement**: a general convex-combination lemma
  (`convexCombo_mem_Icc`) and its specialization to attention
  (`attnOutput_mem_Icc`), showing each coordinate of the output lies in the
  interval spanned by the corresponding coordinates of the value vectors.
* **Log-partition lower bound** (`logPartition_ge_term`): each kernel exponent is
  bounded above by the log-partition function, the `n`-dimensional analogue of the
  two-point `NDimLogSumExp.logsumexp_lower`.
-/

noncomputable section

open Real

namespace SoftmaxAttention

variable {d n : ℕ}

/-- The exponential inner-product kernel `exp ⟪q, k⟫`. -/
noncomputable def expKernel (q k : Fin d → ℝ) : ℝ := Real.exp (∑ i, q i * k i)

/-- The exponential kernel is strictly positive. -/
theorem expKernel_pos (q k : Fin d → ℝ) : 0 < expKernel q k := Real.exp_pos _

/-- The `j`-th softmax attention weight. -/
noncomputable def attnWeight (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) (j : Fin n) : ℝ :=
  expKernel q (ks j) / ∑ k, expKernel q (ks k)

/-- The attention output: a convex combination of value vectors. -/
noncomputable def attnOutput (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks vs : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) : Fin d → ℝ :=
  fun i => ∑ j, attnWeight q ks j * vs j i

/-- The denominator of the softmax (the partition function) is strictly positive
when there is at least one key. -/
theorem sum_expKernel_pos [NeZero n] (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) :
    0 < ∑ k, expKernel q (ks k) := by
  apply Finset.sum_pos
  · intro i _; exact expKernel_pos q (ks i)
  · exact Finset.univ_nonempty

/-- Each attention weight is strictly positive. -/
theorem attnWeight_pos [NeZero n] (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) (j : Fin n) :
    0 < attnWeight q ks j := by
  unfold attnWeight
  exact div_pos (expKernel_pos q (ks j)) (sum_expKernel_pos q ks)

/-- Each attention weight is nonnegative. -/
theorem attnWeight_nonneg [NeZero n] (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) (j : Fin n) :
    0 ≤ attnWeight q ks j := (attnWeight_pos q ks j).le

/-- The attention weights sum to one. -/
theorem attnWeight_sum_one [NeZero n] (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) :
    ∑ j, attnWeight q ks j = 1 := by
  unfold attnWeight
  rw [← Finset.sum_div]
  exact div_self (ne_of_gt (sum_expKernel_pos q ks))

/-- A convex combination of values lying in `[lo, hi]` also lies in `[lo, hi]`. -/
lemma convexCombo_mem_Icc {n : ℕ} (ws : Fin n → ℝ) (xs : Fin n → ℝ) (lo hi : ℝ)
    (hws_nonneg : ∀ j, 0 ≤ ws j)
    (hws_sum : ∑ j, ws j = 1)
    (hxs_bound : ∀ j, lo ≤ xs j ∧ xs j ≤ hi) :
    lo ≤ ∑ j, ws j * xs j ∧ ∑ j, ws j * xs j ≤ hi := by
  constructor
  · calc lo = ∑ j, ws j * lo := by rw [← Finset.sum_mul, hws_sum, one_mul]
      _ ≤ ∑ j, ws j * xs j :=
          Finset.sum_le_sum fun j _ => mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (hxs_bound j).1 (hws_nonneg j)
  · calc ∑ j, ws j * xs j ≤ ∑ j, ws j * hi :=
          Finset.sum_le_sum fun j _ => mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (hxs_bound j).2 (hws_nonneg j)
      _ = hi := by rw [← Finset.sum_mul, hws_sum, one_mul]

/-- **Convex hull confinement**: each coordinate of the attention output lies in the
interval spanned by the corresponding coordinates of the value vectors. -/
theorem attnOutput_mem_Icc [NeZero n] (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks vs : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) (i : Fin d)
    (lo hi : ℝ) (hbound : ∀ j, lo ≤ vs j i ∧ vs j i ≤ hi) :
    lo ≤ attnOutput q ks vs i ∧ attnOutput q ks vs i ≤ hi := by
  unfold attnOutput
  exact convexCombo_mem_Icc (attnWeight q ks) (fun j => vs j i) lo hi
    (attnWeight_nonneg q ks) (attnWeight_sum_one q ks) hbound

/-- **Log-partition lower bound**: each kernel exponent is bounded above by the
log-partition function `log (∑ k, exp ⟪q, kₖ⟫)`. This is the `n`-dimensional
analogue of `NDimLogSumExp.logsumexp_lower`. -/
theorem logPartition_ge_term [NeZero n] (q : Fin d → ℝ) (ks : Fin n → Fin d → ℝ) (j : Fin n) :
    (∑ i, q i * ks j i) ≤ Real.log (∑ k, expKernel q (ks k)) := by
  have hpos : 0 < ∑ k, expKernel q (ks k) := sum_expKernel_pos q ks
  rw [← Real.log_exp (∑ i, q i * ks j i)]
  apply Real.log_le_log (Real.exp_pos _)
  show expKernel q (ks j) ≤ ∑ k, expKernel q (ks k)
  exact Finset.single_le_sum (fun k _ => (expKernel_pos q (ks k)).le) (Finset.mem_univ j)

end SoftmaxAttention

# Computational Evidence — Attention Mechanisms

Concise pre-proof sanity checks for the formal results in this directory.

## 1. Softmax realizes the open simplex (`softmax_realizes_simplex`)
Take `p = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5)`. Then `log p ≈ (-1.609, -1.204, -0.693)`.
`exp(log p) = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5)`, and `∑ exp(log p) = 1`, so
`softmax(log p) = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5) = p`. The identity holds exactly (no temperature),
confirming surjectivity onto the strictly-positive simplex. The boundary (`p_i = 0`)
is unreachable since every softmax weight is `> 0`.

## 2. Attention-sink lower bound (`attention_sink_lower_bound`)
Weights `w_i = exp(z_i)/∑ exp(z_j)` with a dominant token `i₀` having gap `g` over all
others. Bound: `w_{i₀} ≥ 1/(1 + (n-1) e^{-g})`. Small cases:

| n   | g = log n        | (n-1)e^{-g}=(n-1)/n | bound 1/(1+(n-1)/n) |
|-----|------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| 2   | 0.693            | 0.500               | 0.667               |
| 10  | 2.303            | 0.900               | 0.526               |
| 100 | 4.605            | 0.990               | 0.503               |
| 1e6 | 13.816           | ≈1.000              | 0.500⁺              |

So with a *logarithmic* gap `g = log n` the sink keeps `> 1/2` of the attention mass for
every context length — matching `attention_sink_persists`. Without the gap (uniform logits)
each weight is exactly `1/n → 0` (`softmax_uniform`, `softmax_uniform_dilution`).

This is the sharp contrast underlying the "attention sink": dilution `1/n` for generic
tokens vs. `Ω(1)` persistence for a token whose logit lead grows like `log n`.

## 3. Rank collapse (`attnMatrix_constRows_rank_le_one`)
If all queries are identical, every row of the `n×n` attention matrix equals the same
stochastic vector `r`, i.e. `A = 1·rᵀ`, an outer product of rank ≤ 1. Numerically, for
`r = (0.2,0.3,0.5)` the 3×3 matrix with all rows `r` has determinant 0 and a single
nonzero singular value, confirming rank 1.

## 4. Hull confinement (`attnOutput_mem_Icc`)
With values `V = (1, 5, 3)` (one coordinate) and any weights summing to 1, the output
`∑ w_j V_j` always lies in `[1, 5]`; e.g. weights `(0.5,0.1,0.4)` give `2.2 ∈ [1,5]`.
A convex combination cannot escape the coordinatewise min/max — the Nadaraya–Watson
kernel-smoother property.

No counterexamples were found; all conjectures proceeded to formal proof.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Homotopy Type Theory as Foundations: the h-level hierarchy and contractible-fibre
  equivalences, with a Pythagorean bridge

This file develops a small, self-contained fragment of **Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT)**
*inside* Lean 4's intensional type theory and connects it to the **Pythagorean** domain.

We define the bottom of the h-level hierarchy

* `IsContr A`  — `A` is contractible (a centre joined to every point),
* `IsProp  A`  — `A` is a mere proposition (all elements are equal),
* `IsSet   A`  — `A` is a set (all parallel paths are equal),

and the *contractible-fibre* characterisation of equivalences

* `Fiber f b`  — the homotopy fibre `{a // f a = b}`,
* `IsEquiv f`  — every fibre of `f` is contractible.

We prove the foundational facts of univalent foundations that survive in Lean:

* contractible ⇒ proposition ⇒ set (h-level cumulativity);
* singleton / based path spaces are contractible (`isContr_basedPaths`);
* `IsEquiv f ↔ Function.Bijective f` (the bridge between the homotopy-theoretic and
  set-theoretic notions of equivalence);
* `IsEquiv` is closed under identity, composition and the 2-out-of-3 property;
* contractibility/propositionality are invariant under equivalence and closed under
  products and dependent products (`Π`).

## Pythagorean bridge

We instantiate the abstract machinery on the type `PT` of Pythagorean triples
`{(a,b,c) // a² + b² = c²}`.  The arithmetic family `k ↦ (3k, 4k, 5k)` is injective
and lands in `PT`, so by `IsEquiv ↔ Bijective` its range-factorisation is an
equivalence: the natural numbers are homotopy-equivalent to the family of
`(3,4,5)`-multiples (`base345_isEquiv`).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

Hypothesis (H1): the contractible-fibre definition of equivalence agrees with plain
bijectivity in Lean.  Outcome: CONFIRMED (`isEquiv_iff_bijective`).  The forward
direction extracts existence (surjectivity) from each fibre's centre and uniqueness
(injectivity) from each fibre's contraction; the reverse builds the centre from a
surjective witness and the contraction from injectivity.  This is the Lean-survivable
shadow of the HoTT theorem "`f` is an equivalence iff it has contractible fibres".

Hypothesis (H2): h-level cumulativity `IsContr → IsProp → IsSet` holds.  Outcome:
PARTIALLY DEGENERATE.  `IsContr → IsProp` is genuine (`IsContr.isProp`); `IsProp → IsSet`
and indeed `IsSet A` for *every* `A` (`isSet_all`) are provable but collapse to Lean's
definitional proof irrelevance for `Eq` (UIP).  We keep the statements for completeness
and flag the collapse here: in a univalent metatheory `IsSet` would be informative, in
Lean it is not.  The genuinely non-trivial content therefore lives in `IsContr` /
`IsEquiv`, which quantify over *types* (which may be empty or large) rather than over
paths.  Failure analysis: an early attempt to make `IsSet` informative via a custom
`Type`-valued path type was abandoned — without a cubical/observational layer it adds
machinery without escaping UIP.

Outcome: CONFIRMED (`base345_isEquiv`) by reducing to bijectivity (H1) and using that a
range-factorisation is always surjective and is injective exactly when the underlying
map is.  This demonstrates the univalent slogan "equivalent types are interchangeable"
on a concrete arithmetic family: `ℕ ≃ Set.range pt345`.

Insight: the productive boundary in Lean-as-HoTT is the (-2)/(-1)-level data
(`IsContr` / `IsEquiv`), where type-level information is preserved, versus the
0-level (`IsSet`) and above, where Lean's `Prop`-valued `Eq` erases it.

namespace PythHoTT

universe u v w

/-! ## h-levels -/

/-- A type is **contractible** when it has a centre to which every element is equal. -/
def IsContr (A : Type u) : Prop := ∃ a : A, ∀ b, a = b

/-- A type is a **mere proposition** when any two of its elements are equal. -/
def IsProp (A : Type u) : Prop := ∀ a b : A, a = b

/-- A type is a **set** (0-truncated) when any two parallel paths are equal. -/
def IsSet (A : Type u) : Prop := ∀ (a b : A) (p q : a = b), p = q

/-- The homotopy **fibre** of `f` over `b`. -/
def Fiber {A : Type u} {B : Type v} (f : A → B) (b : B) : Type u :=
  {a : A // f a = b}

/-- `f` is an **equivalence** when all of its homotopy fibres are contractible. -/
def IsEquiv {A : Type u} {B : Type v} (f : A → B) : Prop := ∀ b, IsContr (Fiber f b)

/-! ## h-level cumulativity -/

/-- A contractible type is a mere proposition. -/
theorem IsContr.isProp {A : Type u} (h : IsContr A) : IsProp A := by
  intro x y
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h
  rw [← ha x, ← ha y]

/-- Every type is a set in Lean (UIP / definitional proof irrelevance for `Eq`). -/
theorem isSet_all (A : Type u) : IsSet A := by
  intro a b p q
  rfl

/-- A mere proposition is a set. (Degenerate in Lean: see lab notes.) -/
theorem IsProp.isSet {A : Type u} (_h : IsProp A) : IsSet A :=
  isSet_all A

/-! ## Basic contractible / propositional types -/

/-- `PUnit` is contractible. -/
theorem isContr_punit : IsContr (PUnit.{u+1}) :=
  ⟨PUnit.unit, fun _ => rfl⟩

/-- **Singleton contractibility**: the based path space `{b // a = b}` is contractible. -/
theorem isContr_basedPaths {A : Type u} (a : A) : IsContr {b : A // a = b} :=
  ⟨⟨a, rfl⟩, by rintro ⟨b, rfl⟩; rfl⟩

/-- Contractibility is exactly being equivalent to a point. -/
theorem isContr_iff_equiv_punit {A : Type u} :
    IsContr A ↔ Nonempty (A ≃ PUnit.{u+1}) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨a, ha⟩
    exact ⟨{
      toFun := fun _ => PUnit.unit
      invFun := fun _ => a
      left_inv := fun x => ha x
      right_inv := fun _ => rfl }⟩
  · rintro ⟨e⟩
    exact ⟨e.symm PUnit.unit, fun x => e.injective (Subsingleton.elim _ _)⟩

/-! ## Closure properties -/

/-- Contractibility transports across an equivalence. -/
theorem IsContr.of_equiv {A : Type u} {B : Type v} (e : A ≃ B) (h : IsContr A) :
    IsContr B := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h
  refine ⟨e a, fun b => ?_⟩
  rw [← e.apply_symm_apply b, ← ha (e.symm b)]

/-- Propositionality transports across an equivalence. -/
theorem IsProp.of_equiv {A : Type u} {B : Type v} (e : A ≃ B) (h : IsProp A) :
    IsProp B := by
  intro x y
  rw [← e.apply_symm_apply x, ← e.apply_symm_apply y, h (e.symm x) (e.symm y)]

/-- A product of contractible types is contractible. -/
theorem IsContr.prod {A : Type u} {B : Type v} (hA : IsContr A) (hB : IsContr B) :
    IsContr (A × B) := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hA
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := hB
  exact ⟨(a, b), fun p => Prod.ext (ha p.1) (hb p.2)⟩

/-- A dependent product of propositions is a proposition (uses function extensionality). -/
theorem IsProp.pi {A : Type u} {B : A → Type v} (h : ∀ a, IsProp (B a)) :
    IsProp (∀ a, B a) := by
  intro f g
  funext a
  exact h a (f a) (g a)

/-! ## Contractible-fibre equivalences -/

/-- The contractible-fibre definition of equivalence coincides with bijectivity. -/
theorem isEquiv_iff_bijective {A : Type u} {B : Type v} (f : A → B) :
    IsEquiv f ↔ Function.Bijective f := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
    · intro a₁ a₂ h_eq
      obtain ⟨_, hb⟩ := h (f a₁)
      exact congr_arg Subtype.val (hb ⟨a₁, rfl⟩ ▸ hb ⟨a₂, h_eq ▸ rfl⟩)
    · intro b
      obtain ⟨⟨a, ha⟩, _⟩ := h b
      exact ⟨a, ha⟩
  · intro h b
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h.2 b
    refine ⟨⟨a, ha⟩, ?_⟩
    rintro ⟨a', ha'⟩
    exact Subtype.ext (h.1 (ha.trans ha'.symm))

/-- The identity map is an equivalence. -/
theorem isEquiv_id {A : Type u} : IsEquiv (id : A → A) :=
  (isEquiv_iff_bijective id).mpr Function.bijective_id

/-- Equivalences compose. -/
theorem IsEquiv.comp {A : Type u} {B : Type v} {C : Type w}
    {f : A → B} {g : B → C} (hf : IsEquiv f) (hg : IsEquiv g) :
    IsEquiv (g ∘ f) := by
  rw [isEquiv_iff_bijective] at *
  exact hg.comp hf

/-- **2-out-of-3**: if `g ∘ f` and `f` are equivalences then so is `g`. -/
theorem IsEquiv.of_comp_left {A : Type u} {B : Type v} {C : Type w}
    {f : A → B} {g : B → C} (hgf : IsEquiv (g ∘ f)) (hf : IsEquiv f) :
    IsEquiv g := by
  rw [isEquiv_iff_bijective] at *
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · intro b₁ b₂ hb
    obtain ⟨a₁, rfl⟩ := hf.2 b₁
    obtain ⟨a₂, rfl⟩ := hf.2 b₂
    exact congr_arg f (hgf.1 hb)
  · intro c
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hgf.2 c
    exact ⟨f a, ha⟩

/-! ## Pythagorean bridge -/

/-- The predicate carving out Pythagorean triples `a² + b² = c²`. -/
def IsPythagorean (t : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ) : Prop := t.1 ^ 2 + t.2.1 ^ 2 = t.2.2 ^ 2

/-- The type of Pythagorean triples. -/
def PT : Type := {t : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ // IsPythagorean t}

/-- `PT` is a set (degenerate in Lean, see lab notes), recorded for completeness. -/
theorem PT.isSet : IsSet PT :=
  isSet_all PT

/-- The arithmetic `(3,4,5)`-family. -/
def base345 (k : ℕ) : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ := (3 * k, 4 * k, 5 * k)

/-- Every member of the `(3,4,5)`-family is a Pythagorean triple. -/
theorem base345_isPythagorean (k : ℕ) : IsPythagorean (base345 k) :=
  show (3 * k) ^ 2 + (4 * k) ^ 2 = (5 * k) ^ 2 by ring

/-- The `(3,4,5)`-family is injective. -/
theorem base345_injective : Function.Injective base345 := by
  intro x y h
  simp only [base345, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
  omega

/-- The `(3,4,5)`-family as a map into `PT`. -/
def pt345 (k : ℕ) : PT := ⟨base345 k, base345_isPythagorean k⟩

/-- `pt345` is injective. -/
theorem pt345_injective : Function.Injective pt345 :=
  fun _ _ h => base345_injective (Subtype.ext_iff.mp h)

/-- **Pythagorean × HoTT bridge**: the range-factorisation of the `(3,4,5)`-family is
an equivalence (in the contractible-fibre sense), exhibiting `ℕ` as homotopy-equivalent
to the family of `(3,4,5)`-multiples. -/
theorem base345_isEquiv : IsEquiv (Set.rangeFactorization pt345) := by
  rw [isEquiv_iff_bijective]
  refine ⟨?_, Set.rangeFactorization_surjective⟩
  intro a b h
  exact pt345_injective (by simpa using congr_arg Subtype.val h)

end PythHoTT

```
lemma le_closure (gc : GaloisConnection l u) (a : α) : a ≤ u (l a) :=
```

universe u v

section TheoremA

variable {α : Type u} {β : Type v} [CompleteLattice α] [CompleteLattice β]
  {l : α → β} {u : β → α}

/-- The closure operator `u ∘ l` is extensive: `a ≤ u (l a)`. -/
lemma le_closure (gc : GaloisConnection l u) (a : α) : a ≤ u (l a) :=
  gc.le_u_l a

/-- The closure operator `u ∘ l` is idempotent. -/
lemma closure_idem (gc : GaloisConnection l u) (a : α) :
    u (l (u (l a))) = u (l a) :=
  gc.u_l_u_eq_u (l a)

/-- The type of fixed points of the closure operator `u ∘ l`. -/

if every element of `S` is a fixed point of `u ∘ l`, then so is `sInf S`.

  refine' le_antisymm _ _;

  · exact sInf_le ( Set.mem_image_of_mem _ hx );
  · simp_all +decide [ lowerBounds ];
    exact Subtype.mk_le_mk.mpr ( le_sInf fun y hy => by aesop )

  · exact le_trans ( gc.le_u_l a ) h;
  · exact le_trans ( gc.monotone_u ( gc.monotone_l h ) ) x.2.le

lemma coe_sSup (S : Set (Fix gc)) :
    ((sSup S : Fix gc) : α) = u (l (sSup (Subtype.val '' S))) := by
  refine' Eq.symm ( _ : _ = _ );
  convert IsLUB.sSup_eq ( show IsLUB S ( ⟨ u ( l ( sSup ( Subtype.val '' S ) ) ), _ ⟩ : Fix gc ) from _ ) using 1;
  exact ⟨ fun h => Subtype.ext h.symm, fun h => h ▸ rfl ⟩;
  exact gc.u_l_u_eq_u _;
  constructor;
  · intro x hx;
    exact Subtype.mk_le_mk.mpr ( le_trans ( le_sSup ( Set.mem_image_of_mem _ hx ) ) ( gc.le_u_l _ ) );
  · intro x hx;
    refine' Subtype.mk_le_mk.mpr _;
    refine' le_trans _ x.2.le;
    exact gc.monotone_u ( gc.monotone_l ( sSup_le ( Set.forall_mem_image.2 fun y hy => hx hy ) ) )

end Fix

end TheoremA

/-! ## Theorem B — Zariski topology from a Galois connection -/

section TheoremB

open PrimeSpectrum

variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R]

/-- The defining adjunction of the Zariski Galois connection:
`I ≤ vanishingIdeal S ↔ S ⊆ zeroLocus I`. -/
theorem zariski_adjunction (I : Ideal R) (S : Set (PrimeSpectrum R)) :
    I ≤ vanishingIdeal S ↔ S ⊆ zeroLocus (I : Set R) :=
  (subset_zeroLocus_iff_le_vanishingIdeal S I).symm

`Ideal R` and `(Set (PrimeSpectrum R))ᵒᵈ`: the order on the spectrum side is
reversed, reflecting that `zeroLocus` is antitone. -/
theorem zariski_galoisConnection :
    GaloisConnection (α := Ideal R) (β := (Set (PrimeSpectrum R))ᵒᵈ)
      (fun I => zeroLocus (I : Set R)) (fun t => vanishingIdeal t) :=
  PrimeSpectrum.gc R

/-- The upper adjoint is the intersection of the primes:
`vanishingIdeal S = ⨅ p ∈ S, p.asIdeal`. -/
theorem vanishingIdeal_eq_iInf (S : Set (PrimeSpectrum R)) :
    vanishingIdeal S = ⨅ p ∈ S, p.asIdeal := by
  rw [vanishingIdeal]

theorem zariski_closure_eq_radical (I : Ideal R) :
    vanishingIdeal (zeroLocus (I : Set R)) = I.radical :=
  vanishingIdeal_zeroLocus_eq_radical I

/-- Consequently, the fixed points of the Zariski closure operator are exactly the
radical ideals. -/
theorem zariski_fixedPoint_iff_radical (I : Ideal R) :
    vanishingIdeal (zeroLocus (I : Set R)) = I ↔ I.IsRadical := by
  rw [zariski_closure_eq_radical]
  exact ⟨fun h => h ▸ Ideal.radical_isRadical I, fun h => h.radical⟩

end TheoremB

end GaloisLatticeZariskiBridge
